interest: This file illustrates the intense diplomatic, economic, and national security scrutiny focused on Japanese commercial fishing fleets across the Pacific on the eve of World War II. Beyond natural resource preservation in Alaskan salmon fisheries, the records reflect heightened American anxiety that Japanese fishing fleets and floating canneries acted as auxiliary naval reconnaissance units, platforms for espionage, or conduits for covert personnel movement off Alaska, Hawaii, and Mexico. Notably, the report detailing the Mexican government's seizure of the fishing vessels Yoshino and Ryono on December 9, 1941, offers concrete evidence of swift inter-American security coordination in the Pacific within forty-eight hours of Pearl Harbor.
overview: This file comprises two U.S. Department of State "List of Papers" docket sheets (including Form DS-46) from Record Group 59, decimal file 894.628 (Animal Husbandry., Japan, Fisheries. Sponges. Sponge Fisheries.), cataloguing diplomatic correspondence, interdepartmental memoranda, and intelligence reports dated between 1930 and 1942 (with departmental docketing continuing through October 1945). The underlying records track Japanese commercial fishing operations, floating canneries, and maritime vessel movements across the Pacific Basin during the tense period preceding and immediately following the outbreak of the Pacific War. Key subjects include Japanese salmon fishing and cannery vessels off Alaska (particularly Bristol Bay and the Bering Sea) and the Kamchatka Peninsula; domestic food shortages in Japan; national security allegations forwarded by Senator Millard E. Tydings concerning covert crew substitutions on Japanese merchant and fishing vessels; crew nationalities on vessels such as the Amano; legal proceedings in Honolulu; and the surveillance, interception, and eventual seizure of Japanese fishing craft (notably the Yoshino/Joshino and Ryono) by Mexican authorities off the Pacific coast of Mexico in December 1941.

subfiles.about: A State Department docket sheet registering correspondence, reports, and memoranda concerning Japanese fisheries, vessel personnel, and salmon fishing regulations.
subfiles.summary: This docket sheet (designated Exhibit #36, sheet 74) registers correspondence and reports numbered 216 through 225 under decimal file 894.628. It indexes reports by Vice Consul Donald W. Lamm on Japan's marine products industry and Consul Augustus S. Chase on Bering Sea fishing reports in the Manchuria Daily News. It also logs intelligence from Senator Millard E. Tydings alleging covert crew substitutions of Japanese fishing crews via merchant vessels, War Department notices regarding Danish mariner Christian Albertsen leaving the all-Japanese crewed vessel Amano, diplomatic dispatches from Mexico concerning the detention of the fishing boats Yoshino and Ryono, and reports on Japanese fish shortages and Kamchatka salmon fisheries involving the Department of the Interior and the Office of Censorship.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Fisheries - Japan (Entries 216-225)

subfiles.about: A State Department Form DS-46 docket sheet recording military, naval, and Treasury intelligence regarding Japanese fishing fleets and vessels in Alaska, Hawaii, and Mexico.
subfiles.summary: This register sheet catalogues entries 241 through 244 under the heading "Fishing vessels --- Japan." It records Coast Guard reports from August 1940 tracking the Japanese floating cannery Kosai Maru accompanied by nine 100-ton fishing craft off Alaska, Navy Department reports on fishing vessel operations in Bristol Bay in June 1941, and Treasury Department reports on cases pending against Japanese vessels in the U.S. District Court in Honolulu. The final entry notes a paraphrased dispatch from the U.S. Naval Attaché in Mexico City reporting the Mexican government's seizure of the Japanese vessels Joshino (Yoshino) and Ryono on December 9, 1941, two days after the attack on Pearl Harbor.
subfiles.title: Department of State List of Papers: Fishing vessels - Japan (Entries 241-244)
